## How git worktrees work

A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository in a different directory. Every worktree shares one `.git` database, so commits, branches, and stashes are visible everywhere. Each worktree holds its own working files and its own `HEAD`.

- Git allows a branch to be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
- Creating a worktree costs a directory of files, not a full clone.
- Deleting a worktree folder does not delete its branch. Run `git worktree prune` to clear stale entries.

```bash
# Create a worktree on a new branch, based on main
git worktree add ../demo-fix -b fix/typo main

# List every checkout and the branch it holds
git worktree list

# Remove the worktree when finished (branch stays)
git worktree remove ../demo-fix
```

| Task | Without worktrees | With worktrees |
|---|---|---|
| Review a PR while your feature branch has uncommitted work | Stash, switch, switch back | Open a second directory |
| Run a long build on `main` | Blocks your editor's branch | Runs in its own folder |
| Compare two branches side by side | Two clones | One repo, two folders |

Use worktrees when you need two branches open at once. Plain branch switching is enough for quick, sequential work.

I'm drafting the story now: a lighthouse keeper named Iris Calloway who has tended Harrow Point for nineteen years, with the automation crew arriving in March to replace her station, a young worker named Teo offering her a plaque, and now October arriving with the crew gone and the new controller humming in her place.

On the ninth night the fog rolls in thick, the controller flashes an unfamiliar fault code, and Iris hears a small fishing boat struggling home through the swell -- echoing the memory of her husband, who made this same journey for twenty-two years until the night he didn't return. The machine insists everything is fine, but she knows the boat out there has no way of knowing that.

So she goes down to the storeroom, greases the old manual shutter crank by hand, and climbs back to the lantern room to do what the controller can't -- she flashes the spare lamp toward the engine noise, three long and one short, the old signal her husband taught her, until the boat finally slides safely into the harbor. Shaking, she drinks her cold coffee and later writes in the paper logbook: *Fog. Boat home. Light held.* -- underlining the last two words twice.

# The last watch

Iris Calloway had kept the Harrow Point light for nineteen years, and in all that time the sea never asked her a question. It came in and went out. The light turned every eleven seconds. She counted them the way other people counted breaths.

The automation crew arrived in March. Two men in orange vests, a tablet with a green progress bar, and a helicopter that hovered over the rocks like a nervous insect. They told her the station would run itself by autumn. They were polite about it. One of them, a young man named Teo, asked whether she would like a plaque.

"For what?" she said.

"For the service."

She looked at him for a while. Then she made the coffee the way her mother had, in the dented steel pot that was older than the lamp.

Now it was October, and the crew had gone. The new controller hummed in the lantern room, a gray box bolted to the iron where her logbook used to sit. Every night she checked it. Every night it reported normal. Every night she felt slightly more useless, which she had not expected.

On the ninth night the fog came in thick. The horn sounded from the bell buoy, stopped, then sounded again. The controller displayed a fault code she didn't recognize. Iris stood with one hand on the cold glass and listened.

Somewhere past the reef, a small boat was coming home late. She could hear its engine, thin and uncertain, rising and falling with the swell. The fishing boats from the village always came back this way in fog. Her husband had been one of them. He came home in fog for twenty-two years, until the night he didn't.

The controller said everything was fine. It was probably right. The light was turning, the lens was clean, and the mechanism had no reason to fail.

But the boat did not know that. It needed to see a light where a light should be, and the lens could only give it one if someone kept it honest.

Iris went down the iron stairs, counting the steps out of habit. In the storeroom she found the old manual crank for the backup shutter, the one nobody had oiled in a decade. She worked grease into it with a rag. Her knuckles ached. She didn't stop.

Then she climbed back up, sat beside the controller, and did the one thing it could not do. She watched the fog. When the engine noise drifted closer, she flashed the spare lamp toward the sound, slow and steady: three long and one short. It was the signal her husband had taught her, the one that meant *come home*.

It took forty minutes. At the end, a red and green hull slid into the harbor mouth, and a man on the deck raised an arm.

Iris set the lamp down. Her hands shook. She poured the cold coffee into her mug anyway and drank it standing, looking out at the water.

In the morning she wrote in the paper logbook that nobody had asked her to keep. *Fog. Boat home. Light held.* Then she underlined the last two words twice, the way you mark something you intend to remember.
